clue.text: They are smokers in the main

definitions.text: They are smokers in the main

parts.words: They are smokers in the main
parts.note: the smokers are vessels puffing out smoke from their funnels, and the main is the open sea they sail on

explanation.surface: A remark about people who mostly smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' reads as 'mostly', but the main is the sea; the smokers are coal-fired ships with funnels.
explanation.definitionFit: Vessels driven by boilers send smoke from their funnels as they cross the sea.

clue.text: Boom in coins, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of coins might be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A boom in coin collecting, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges COINS; the definition means boom as in 'sonic boom', with 'in' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective names what relates to sound, as in the shock wave of a sonic boom.

clue.text: Odd that the nave's to one side

definitions.meaning: the hub of a wheel is called its nave, so a wheel whose hub sits off-centre is out of true

explanation.surface: Something strange about a church whose nave is off to one side.
explanation.walkthrough: The nave suggests a church, but a nave is also the hub of a wheel; when it is to one side the wheel is off-centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange people are off-centre, and a wheel with its hub displaced is literally off its centre.

clue.text: Whereby to sing the praises of decimalization?

definitions.text: Whereby to sing the praises of decimalization?

parts.words: Whereby to sing the praises of decimalization?
parts.note: decimal measures are metric, so hymns praising them would be songs about the metric system

explanation.surface: Asking how to celebrate the switch to decimal currency.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain decimalized its currency in 1971; metrical psalms are psalms set in verse for singing, and 'metrical' puns on metric.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalms translated into rhymed verse for congregational singing are named for their regular metre.

clue.text: The work of a pack of snobs ?

definitions.text: The work of a pack of snobs ?

parts.words: The work of a pack of snobs ?
parts.note: snob is an old word for a cobbler, and part of a cobbler's job is fixing the backs of shoes

explanation.surface: What a group of social climbers gets up to.
explanation.walkthrough: A snob was once a shoemaker; heeling is putting heels on shoes. It is also what hounds do in a pack, following at heel.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitting new heels to shoes is a cobbler's work, and snob is an old word for a cobbler.

clue.text: It's mortifying that the last letter has left the Corn: sh town

indicators.note: the named letter departs from the place name, so the word is shortened

parts.note: Penzance is a seaside town at the western tip of Cornwall
Z is the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Embarrassment that the final letter has left a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has left' takes Z, the alphabet's last letter, out of PENZANCE, a town at the far western tip of Cornwall in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-punishment for sin is a mortification, something that humbles the flesh.

clue.text: Bard of the Jerusalem mosque

definitions.meaning: a poet, here the Persian author of the Rubaiyat, Khayyam
the Dome of the Rock is popularly called the Mosque of the caliph who first built a prayer house on the site

explanation.surface: A poet attached to a famous mosque in Jerusalem.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Omar Khayyam; the Dome of the Rock is often called the Mosque of Omar after the second caliph.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian poet of the Rubaiyat shares his first name with the caliph honoured in a Jerusalem mosque's popular title.

clue.text: Bird in the hand? Palm, rather

definitions.meaning: a large brightly coloured tropical parrot
a tropical American palm tree shares the bird's name

explanation.surface: A bird held in the hand, or perhaps the palm of the hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the hand' sets up the proverb and makes 'Palm' read as part of the hand; it is a palm tree named after the parrot.
explanation.definitionFit: A large tropical parrot and the spiny palm tree named after it share one word.

clue.text: Ringing the changes on a screen

indicators.note: ringing the changes is a bellringer's term for varying the order, so the letters run in a new sequence

explanation.surface: Trying every variation on a display screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing the changes' is a single idiom on the surface; split, 'the changes' rearranges ON A SCREEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Echoing, prolonged sound is a reverberation, the quality of a bell still sounding.

clue.text: But he's not commissioned to make a militant harangue

definitions.text: But he's not commissioned to make a militant harangue

parts.words: But he's not commissioned to make a militant harangue
parts.note: read as war plus rant, the rank sounds like an officer charged with ranting about war, yet the rank holds no commission

explanation.surface: A soldier reminded he has no authority to give a warlike speech.
explanation.walkthrough: A militant harangue is a war rant; this rank sits below commissioned officers, holding a warrant instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Armed forces rank holding a warrant rather than a commission, above sergeants but below lieutenants.

clue.text: It's often put on as an educational show

definitions.text: It's often put on as an educational show

parts.words: It's often put on as an educational show
parts.note: an old school one is worn round the collar to display which school the wearer attended

explanation.surface: A school play or lesson that is often staged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' and 'show' suggest staging a production, but the item is worn: an old school tie displays your education.
explanation.definitionFit: An old school tie is a piece of neckwear worn to display where its owner was educated.

clue.text: Shades of Paris!

parts.note: the English word for subtle shades of colour or meaning is borrowed from French, so these are shades that come from Paris

explanation.surface: An exclamation recalling Paris, as in 'shades of the old days'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shades of ...!' is an idiom for being reminded of something; here it means literal shades, a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtle gradations of tone or meaning are called by a word taken straight from French.

clue.text: State provision

definitions.meaning: a state of affairs or health
a stipulation or proviso in a contract

explanation.definitionFit: Both a state of being and a stipulation laid down in an agreement share this one word.

clue.text: Could be a war on in Mountain Ash

indicators.note: the letters of 'war on' could be rearranged into another word, so the phrase signals a reshuffle

explanation.surface: A war might break out in a place called Mountain Ash.
explanation.walkthrough: Mountain Ash is also a Welsh town, which gives the war its setting; 'Could be' rearranges WAR ON.
explanation.definitionFit: The mountain ash is the common name for the tree with red berries, also called the quickbeam.

clue.text: Leave car with a jacket and hood

parts.note: to leave a car somewhere is to park it

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the car and takes a hooded jacket along.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak-style coat is a hooded weatherproof jacket.

clue.text: Spears for one side only?

definitions.meaning: supporters strongly committed to a single faction

explanation.surface: Weapons meant for a single side.
explanation.walkthrough: A partisan is both a medieval polearm and a committed supporter of one side.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval polearm and a committed adherent of a faction share one word.

clue.text: As played by the inexperienced musician?

definitions.text: As played by the inexperienced musician?

parts.words: As played by the inexperienced musician?
parts.note: a novice is called green, so the brass instrument a novice plays would be a ...

explanation.surface: A question about what a beginner musician plays.
explanation.walkthrough: Green means inexperienced, so the novice's instrument is a green horn, and a greenhorn is a novice.
explanation.definitionFit: A beginner or raw recruit lacking experience is called by this name, made of 'green' and a brass instrument.

clue.text: Arrange it on a tree to get bearings

indicators.note: arranging the words means setting their letters in a new order

explanation.surface: Climbing a tree to work out where you are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrange' rearranges IT ON A TREE.
explanation.definitionFit: To find which way one faces is to establish one's position, as with a compass.

clue.text: Social occasion spoilt by interference

definitions.meaning: a formal party at which guests are welcomed
radio or television signal quality, which interference spoils

explanation.definitionFit: A formal welcoming party and the quality of a broadcast signal share one word.

clue.text: Narrow-minded, not joining the Continent?

definitions.meaning: like an island, cut off from the mainland of Europe

explanation.surface: A dig at Britons who refuse to join Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin for island gives the sense of being cut off from the mainland, as Britain is from the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: An islander's outlook is parochial, and an island stands apart from any mainland.

clue.text: The price of arrogance

parts.note: in Greek myth hubris is punished by a goddess of retribution, whose name now means inescapable downfall

explanation.surface: What pride costs.
explanation.walkthrough: Nemesis was the Greek goddess who punished hubris; her name now means downfall that pride brings.
explanation.definitionFit: Retribution follows pride, as the Greek goddess of vengeance punished human hubris.

clue.text: Oil-producer under pressure

parts.note: the fruit that yields oil when it is crushed in a press

explanation.surface: An oil company or oil state facing pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under pressure' suggests a stressed oil company, but it means the fruit yields its oil when pressed.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit of the Mediterranean tree is pressed to extract its cooking oil.

clue.text: The end of Forster's passage

parts.note: E. M. Forster's novel is A Passage to ..., so the end of the passage is its destination and the title's last word

explanation.surface: Where a piece of Forster's writing finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: E. M. Forster wrote the novel A Passage to India; the passage's end is both its destination and the title's last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The destination of the journey named in Forster's novel title is the subcontinent.

clue.text: Senior postman has that " same again " yearning

parts.note: do, short for ditto, means the same again in a list
a yen is a longing

explanation.surface: An old postman who longs to do the same again.
explanation.walkthrough: DO is ditto, the mark for 'same again'; the senior postman is the doyen, the longest-serving member of a body.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest-serving member of any group, such as the post office staff, is its most senior figure.

clue.text: Stage four reached before the last meeting

definitions.text: Stage four reached before the last meeting

parts.words: Stage four reached before the last meeting
parts.note: in a knockout, the round contested by the last four competitors comes just before the final match

explanation.surface: A fourth step reached ahead of a final meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage four' reads as the fourth step, but it is the stage four competitors reach, just before the final.
explanation.definitionFit: The round of a knockout competition played among the last four, leading to the final.

clue.text: Vegetables in need of a plug, we hear ?

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by how it is said aloud

parts.note: pipes or vessels that leak need plugging

explanation.surface: Vegetables that seem to need a plug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' sounds LEAKS, which need plugging, as the vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Long white-stemmed onions are a staple vegetable, the national emblem of Wales.

clue.text: Lamb, say, is uncommonly unfathomable

indicators.note: uncommonly means in an unusual way, so the letters are set out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Charles Lamb, for instance, is extraordinarily deep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' rearranges LAMB and SAY; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An abyss is a bottomless chasm, so something as deep as one cannot be fathomed or measured.

clue.text: Plundering, in the days when Falstaff drank

parts.note: Falstaff, Shakespeare's tippler, drinks sack, a dry white wine
the days of an era make an age

explanation.surface: A remark about Falstaff's drinking days that hides plunder.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is the fortified wine Shakespeare's Falstaff drinks; the age of sack gives SACK+AGE, an old word for the sacking of a town.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacking a city is pillaging it, and this archaic noun names that pillage.

clue.text: Founder of a place of iniquity

definitions.meaning: a verb: a ship founders when it fills and goes down
a den of vice, as in the phrase a ... of iniquity

explanation.surface: The founder of a den of vice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founder' reads as the person who started something, but it is the verb for a ship going down.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship that founders goes under, and a sink of iniquity is a den of vice.

clue.text: Not that the wild-life ones use life ones

definitions.text: Not that the wild-life ones use life ones

parts.words: Not that the wild-life ones use life ones
parts.note: conservationists who protect wildlife share a name with the lifebelts and coshes called life ones, though they need neither

explanation.surface: A wry aside that conservationists do not carry lifebelts.
explanation.walkthrough: Wildlife conservationists and life-savers (a lifebelt, or a cosh, called a life preserver) share the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: People who protect wildlife are called its keepers or protectors, and lifebelts and coshes share that name.
